newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese broker Yamaichi posts small pretax profit.
newsitem.headline: Japanese broker Yamaichi posts small pretax profit.

text.p: Japan's fourth-biggest brokerage Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd said on Monday that it posted a small pre-tax profit in the last business year, but aid to an affiliate pushed it into the red on a net basis.
Yamaichi's business results came after the other three of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages announced last week that aid to troubled affiliates also put them into the red on a net basis for 1996/97.
Yamaichi said it posted parent current profits of 1.22 billion yen ($9.6 million) for the year ended March 31, down 91.9 percent from a year earlier.

But its parent net loss totalled 164.76 billion yen ($1.30 billion), largely due to a special loss of 150 billion yen ($1.19 billion) resulting from aid to a troubled financial affiliate, Yamaichi said.
Current profit is pre-tax profit and includes gains and losses made on securities investments and other non-operating activities.

Yamaichi vice-president Ryuji Shirai told a news conference that Yamaichi took out 43 billion yen ($341 million) in subordinated loans in 1996/97 to make up for a decline in capital as a result of the net loss.

Analysts said the three other big brokers -- Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd -- also took out subordinated loans to minimise a drop in capital as such loans are calculated as a part of capital.
While Nomura Securities posted a healthy 35.7 percent year-on-year increase in parent current profit, Daiwa and Nikko posted year-on-year declines.
However, they also recorded net losses in 1996/97 due to financial aid to their affiliates.

Japan's securities industry suffered a major setback last month after Nomura said two of its directors were involved in suspected illegal deals in which substantial sums of Nomura money were moved to the account of a corporate customer who was linked to a "sokaiya" racketeer.
Japanese media have reported that the corporate customer in the Nomura scandal also has accounts at other big brokers.
Shirai said that Yamaichi was conducting an in-house investigation again after similar checks last month. He declined to give further details.
Last month, he told reporters that an internal investigation had not found any accounts linking the firm to sokaiya racketeers.

Shirai also again denied media reports that Yamaichi had conducted illegal "tobashi" deals, in which brokers seek to hide a client's investment losses by transferring them to another client's account.
"This is not a fact. We filed libel suits against a Japanese magazine (on Friday last week)," he said.
Yamaichi declined to forecast its earnings for the current business year, saying that it will start announcing its earnings on a quarterly basis from now on.
But Shirai said he expected daily average turnover on the Tokyo Stock Exchange to be about 400 billion yen ($3.17 billion) in 1997/98, little changed from the last business year.
